q: A new hybrid team keeps dropping work at the handoff between the design and build groups. Which two actions should the project manager take first?
options: Facilitate a session where the team agrees handoff rules and adds them to the team charter
Replace the design lead with someone more experienced
Run a retrospective on the handoff problem and let the team choose improvements to try
Report each member's missed handoffs to their functional manager
Add a daily written status report from each group
explain: The team owns how it works together, so the project manager facilitates: agree working rules (team charter) and let the team inspect and adapt (retrospective). Replacing people or reporting them to managers skips coaching and damages trust. More status reports add overhead without fixing the handoff.

q: Two team members disagree openly about the testing approach, and the dispute is slowing the work. Put the project manager's steps in order.
options: Bring them together to focus on the shared goal and the facts
Follow up later to check the agreement is working
Talk with each person privately to understand their position
Help them agree on an approach they can both support
explain: Understand first (private conversations), then collaborate on the facts and shared goal, reach a solution both support, and confirm it holds. Jumping straight to a joint meeting, or deciding for them, tends to harden positions instead of solving the problem.

q: During execution, an influential stakeholder who was never in the stakeholder register starts objecting to deliverables. Which two actions are best?
options: Ignore the objections because the requirements were already signed off
Add the stakeholder to the register and analyse their interest and influence
Ask the sponsor to keep the stakeholder away from the project
Meet the stakeholder to understand their concerns and agree how they will be engaged
Stop all work until the stakeholder approves every deliverable
explain: A missed stakeholder is identified late, not ignored: record and analyse them, then engage them directly to understand concerns. Ignoring or blocking an influential stakeholder raises risk; halting all work is an overreaction before you know what the concerns are.

q: A team member in a distant time zone keeps missing key decisions made in live meetings. Which two actions should the project manager take?
options: Require the member to attend every meeting at head-office time
Review the communications plan with the team, for example rotating meeting times
Leave the member out of decisions to avoid delays
Record decisions in a shared written log that everyone can read and comment on
Send more emails so nothing is missed
explain: Fix the communication approach for a distributed team: adjust the plan so the burden is shared, and make decisions visible asynchronously. Forcing one person to bear the cost or excluding them hurts engagement; more email adds volume, not clarity.

q: On a predictive project, a stakeholder asks to change an approved deliverable. Put the project manager's steps in order.
options: Take it to the change control board for a decision
Log the change request
Update the plans and tell stakeholders the decision
Analyse the impact on scope, schedule, cost and risk
explain: Integrated change control: record the request, assess its impact, get a decision from whoever has authority (often a change control board), then update the baselines and plans and communicate. Analysing before logging, or updating plans before approval, bypasses control.

q: A supplier warns that a key component may arrive three weeks late. Which two actions should the project manager take?
options: Update the risk register and assess the schedule impact
Cancel the contract and find a new supplier
Work with the supplier on a response, such as a partial early delivery
Wait until the delay is confirmed before doing anything
Tell the team to start working overtime now
explain: The delay is still uncertain, so treat it as a risk: record and analyse it, then plan a response with the supplier. Cancelling the contract is drastic and may breach it; waiting loses response time; overtime now spends money on a delay that may not happen.

q: Put these risk management activities in the order they normally happen.
options: Plan responses for the highest-priority risks
Identify risks with the team and stakeholders
Monitor the risks and how well the responses work
Analyse and prioritise the risks
Implement the agreed responses when needed
explain: Identify and analyze risks, plan responses, implement them at the appropriate time, and monitor effectiveness. Some responses act before an event occurs; contingent responses follow agreed triggers. The cycle repeats throughout delivery.

q: Midway through a sprint, the product owner asks the team to add an urgent new feature. Which two responses fit agile practice?
options: Add it to the product backlog so the product owner can order it for an upcoming sprint
Have the project manager tell the team to work overtime to fit it in
Quietly add it to the sprint without changing anything else
If it cannot wait, the product owner and team agree to swap it for not-yet-started work of similar size, keeping the sprint goal
Extend the sprint by a week to make room
explain: New work normally goes to the product backlog, ordered by the product owner. If it truly cannot wait, scope inside the sprint can be renegotiated between the product owner and team as long as the sprint goal holds. Sprints are fixed timeboxes, so extending one is wrong; overtime and silent additions break sustainable pace and transparency.

q: Put these Scrum events in the order they happen within one sprint.
options: Sprint review
Daily scrums
Sprint retrospective
Sprint planning
explain: Within the containing Sprint event, Sprint Planning initiates the Sprint; Daily Scrums help Developers inspect and adapt during the work; Sprint Review inspects the outcome with stakeholders; Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint.

q: The customer finds several defects in a deliverable that passed internal testing. Which two actions should the project manager take?
options: Analyse the root cause of the defects with the team
Tell the customer the deliverable already passed testing
Improve the test approach so this kind of defect is caught earlier
Add one more inspection only at final delivery
Ask the customer to accept the defects to protect the schedule
explain: Find out why the defects escaped and improve the process: prevention over inspection. Defending the old test result or pressing the customer to accept defects ignores quality; a single extra inspection at the end catches problems late, when they cost most to fix.

q: At midpoint, CPI is 0.85 and SPI is 1.05. Which two interpretations of these EVM ratios are correct?
options: The project is over budget for the work completed
The project is behind schedule
Earned work value exceeds planned work value at this date
The project is under budget
Both cost and schedule are exactly on plan
explain: CPI below 1 indicates unfavorable cost efficiency for work completed. SPI above 1 means EV exceeds PV at this date; it does not establish that the critical path is ahead or that the project will finish early.

q: A new data-protection regulation will take effect before your product launches. Which two actions should the project manager take?
options: Continue as planned because the project was approved before the law passed
Assess the regulation's impact on requirements, scope and schedule with compliance experts
Wait for an audit to see whether anything needs to change
Raise a change request for the changes needed to comply
Leave compliance to the vendor that builds the product
explain: External regulatory change is part of the business environment the project manager must watch. Assess the impact with the right experts, then manage the needed changes through change control. Ignoring it, waiting for an audit, or handing accountability to a vendor leaves the organisation exposed.

q: Which two findings mean the project should be re-evaluated against its business case?
options: The market need the project was meant to meet has disappeared
A team member has resigned
A minor defect was found in testing
The expected benefits are now lower than the cost to finish
A non-critical task slipped by two days
explain: The business case justifies the project by its value. If the need is gone or remaining cost now exceeds the benefits, the sponsor must decide whether to continue, change or stop. Staffing changes, minor defects and small slips are normal project issues, managed inside the project.

q: On the PMP exam, which two choices usually reflect the best project manager response to a problem?
options: Escalate to the sponsor straight away
Assess the situation and gather the facts before acting
Follow the plan exactly, whatever has changed
Address the issue directly with the people involved before escalating
Make a quick decision alone to avoid delay
explain: The exam favours a project manager who understands the situation first, then works with the people involved and escalates only when it is beyond their authority. Escalating at once, rigidly following an outdated plan, or deciding alone usually signal a wrong answer.
